question_text:
Text 1
Sediment cores drilled from the floor of Vellmar Basin, a deep fjord, show paired layers: a pale layer laid down each summer and a dark layer laid down each winter. Between 1840 and 1900 the dark layers are about twice as thick as those from the decades before and after. The dark layers are mostly fine clay, which rivers carry into the basin. The explanation is a run of unusually wet winters that swelled the rivers feeding the fjord. A smaller share of each dark layer is organic matter from plankton blooms, but the extra clay accounts for the thickening.

Text 2
The thickening of the dark layers between 1840 and 1900 is well documented, and the layers do consist chiefly of winter clay. Yet the clay may have reached the core sites in greater amounts without any increase in river flow. If the bottom currents in the basin shifted around 1840, they could have swept clay from the surrounding slopes toward the drilled locations and left it there in thicker deposits. Cores taken farther across the basin, which have not yet been analyzed, would help show whether the thickening was basin-wide or confined to the sites sampled so far.

Based on the texts, how do the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 differ in their treatment of the thickened dark layers in the Vellmar Basin cores?
answer_a: Text 2 accepts that the layers are mostly clay, but it suggests that the clay came from plankton blooms rather than from rivers.
answer_b: Text 2 questions whether the thickening extends beyond the sampled sites, but it agrees that swollen rivers delivered the clay.
answer_c: Text 2 accepts the thickening that Text 1 reports, but it suggests that wetter winters may be only part of why the clay accumulated.
answer_d: Text 2 accepts the thickening that Text 1 reports, but it suggests that a different process may have delivered the clay to the core sites.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. Text 1 reports that the dark layers thickened between 1840 and 1900 and explains the change as extra clay delivered by swollen rivers. Text 2 grants the observation, calling the thickening well documented and the layers chiefly winter clay. It then offers a hedged alternative about why the clay built up: shifted bottom currents may have swept clay toward the drilled locations without any increase in river flow. The authors therefore agree about what the cores show and differ about the process that delivered the clay.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It borrows the plankton detail from Text 1, where organic matter is only a smaller share of each dark layer. Text 2 grants that the layers consist chiefly of clay and proposes that shifted currents moved that clay, not that plankton supplied it.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. Text 2 does note that cores from farther across the basin could show whether the thickening was basin-wide, so it leaves its extent open, but it does not agree that swollen rivers delivered the clay. It proposes that the clay may have arrived with no increase in river flow.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It treats Text 2 as adding to Text 1's explanation. Text 2 offers shifted currents as a way for the clay to accumulate without any increase in river flow, so it presents its idea in place of Text 1's cause rather than as a further part of it.

question_text:
Text 1
Along a former lagoon shore at Quarry Ridge, paleontologists have mapped eleven parallel sauropod trackways, all heading north. The mapping was careful: every print was measured and its heading recorded. The prints are spaced at nearly even intervals, and the smallest prints lie nearer the center of the group than its edges. Such order is unlikely to arise by chance. Animals crossing a landscape alone tend to wander, but these animals kept pace with one another and sheltered their young between larger adults, much as living herds of large mammals move. The trackways therefore record a single herd traveling together across the shore.

Text 2
The mapping at Quarry Ridge is careful, and the alignment of the trackways is real. Yet the prints were pressed into a strip of firm mud only a few dozen meters wide, hemmed in by the lagoon on one side and a dune ridge on the other. Animals walking that strip separately, perhaps days apart, could also have left parallel, evenly spaced tracks, since the terrain left them little room to do otherwise, and the central position of the smaller prints might reflect where the mud was firmest. The prints record where each animal stepped but not when. Any firm conclusion about how these animals came to leave the prints would have to rest on more than the prints' arrangement.

Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would likely view the evidence in Text 1?
answer_a: The trackway measurements are accurate, but they fit both a traveling herd and separate animals following the same strip, so they cannot by themselves decide between those accounts.
answer_b: The trackway measurements are accurate, but they describe how the animals moved along the shore, so they bear little on why those animals were on the strip together.
answer_c: The trackway measurements are accurate, but the narrowness of the strip makes them better explained by separate animals walking alone than by a herd traveling together.
answer_d: The trackway measurements are accurate, but the prints were probably recorded in too few places to support any conclusion about whether the animals moved together.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. Text 2 grants that the mapping is careful and the alignment is real, so it treats Text 1's evidence as sound. It then offers a second account that the same prints would fit: animals passing separately through a narrow strip of mud that left them little room to do otherwise. Because the prints show where each animal stepped but not when, Text 2 adds that any firm conclusion "would have to rest on more than the prints' arrangement," so the pattern cannot settle between the herd account and the separate-passage account. The author of Text 2 would therefore view the evidence as genuine but unable, on its own, to choose between the two explanations.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It is true that the prints record movement, but Text 2 does not call the evidence beside the point. It uses the same alignment and spacing as the common ground for two accounts of whether the animals traveled together, so the evidence bears directly on the question, just not decisively.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. Text 2 does mention the narrow strip, but it offers it as a reason the separate-passage account is possible, not as a reason that account is the better one. Text 2 says only that separate animals "could also" have left such tracks and that a firm conclusion needs more than the arrangement, so it does not take the evidence to favor either account.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Text 2 calls the mapping careful and never questions how many places were sampled or how the prints were recorded. Its limit on the evidence concerns what the prints can show (where, not when), not how thoroughly they were collected.

question_text:
Text 1
Translation scholars have observed that later translations of a work tend to stay closer to the original's phrasing than earlier ones do. The first translator must make an unfamiliar work welcome and so smooths over its strangeness; once readers know the work, later translators can afford to let that strangeness show. The English versions of the Tessaly Chronicle, a medieval history from the Adriatic coast, bear this out. The 1891 version turns the author's blunt proverbs into polished English maxims, while the 1978 and 2011 versions keep the proverbs' odd imagery nearly intact.

Text 2
The later English versions of the Tessaly Chronicle do keep more of the original's phrasing, and the proverbs are a fair sample of the change. Yet the 1891 translator worked from a single damaged manuscript whose lines were often unreadable, and smoothing may have been the only way to produce a continuous text. A critical edition reconciling the surviving copies appeared in 1952, and the later translators drew on it throughout. It may be that close rendering became feasible only once the text itself was settled. Few works are preserved so poorly at the outset.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim about later translations in Text 1?
answer_a: Text 2 would grant that the pattern holds for translations generally, but would suggest that the Chronicle's later versions owe their closeness to a cause other than the one Text 1 gives.
answer_b: Text 2 would grant that later translations generally stay closer to the original, but would suggest that the Chronicle's later versions do not actually show that pattern.
answer_c: Text 2 would grant that the Chronicle's later versions stay closer to the original, but would suggest a cause tied to the Chronicle's unusual textual history, leaving open whether the pattern holds for translations generally.
answer_d: Text 2 would deny that later translations generally stay closer to the original, but would suggest that the Chronicle's later versions show that pattern by coincidence.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. Text 1 states a general principle (later translations stay closer to the original because readers already know the work) and offers the Chronicle as a case. Text 2 first accepts the case: the later versions "do keep more of the original's phrasing." It then offers a reason tied to this particular work: the 1891 translator faced a single damaged manuscript, and close rendering "may" have become feasible only after the 1952 critical edition settled the text. Text 2 adds that "few works are preserved so poorly at the outset," so that cause need not apply to other works. Text 2 therefore neither confirms nor refutes the general principle. It only shows that the Chronicle does not by itself prove it.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It correctly has Text 2 offering a different cause for the Chronicle, but it credits Text 2 with accepting the principle as true of translations generally. Text 2 says nothing to establish that; by tying the change to the manuscript and the 1952 edition, it leaves the principle's generality unsupported rather than granted.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It correctly treats Text 2 as not rejecting the principle outright, but it misplaces the disagreement on the case. Text 2 explicitly concedes that the later versions keep more of the original's phrasing and calls the proverbs a fair sample, so it does not claim the Chronicle fails to show the pattern.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It correctly notes that Text 2 offers an explanation for the Chronicle other than Text 1's, but it turns this into a denial of the general principle and calls the result a coincidence. Text 2 only suggests the cause "may" be the settled text; it never argues that later translations generally fail to stay closer, and it attributes the change to a specific reason rather than chance.

question_text:
Text 1
Elbow injuries among players aged eleven and twelve have climbed in recent seasons, and the cause is not mysterious. The ligaments in a growing arm seldom fail from one violent throw; instead, they weaken as thousands of ordinary, high-effort throws pile up, each leaving a small amount of strain that the arm has not yet repaired. Leagues should therefore cap each pitcher at seventy-five pitches per game. Enforcing such a cap is simple, since volunteer scorekeepers already count pitches during games and would need no new training to apply a limit.

Text 2
Pitch limits of the kind proposed deserve a closer look. In many communities, eleven- and twelve-year-olds pitch for a school-league team and a travel team in the same week, and a per-game cap treats a player who throws seventy pitches on Saturday and seventy more on Sunday no differently from one who throws seventy once. League officials might find that a pitcher's total over a week gives a more informative picture, though gathering those totals across separate teams would be difficult, and no study has yet compared the two approaches directly. Until such evidence exists, it seems premature to treat a per-game cap as the measure best suited to the problem.

Which idea in Text 1 must the author of Text 2 accept for Text 2's objection to a per-game cap to make sense?
answer_a: Leagues should cap young pitchers at a fixed number of pitches in each individual game they pitch.
answer_b: Injury to a young pitcher's elbow results from the buildup of many ordinary throws rather than from one forceful throw.
answer_c: Volunteer scorekeepers who already count pitches in games would not need extra training to enforce a cap.
answer_d: A pitcher's throws across separate games in the same week should be added together to judge the strain on the arm.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. Text 2 never states why Saturday and Sunday outings should be considered together, but its objection only makes sense if strain accumulates from repeated throws: a pitcher who throws seventy pitches on two consecutive days is at greater risk than one who throws seventy once only if the arm's risk depends on the buildup of throws. That is the premise Text 1 supplies when it says ligaments weaken as many ordinary throws pile up rather than failing from one violent throw. Text 2 uses this idea silently as the basis for questioning the per-game cap, so its author must accept it.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This is the conclusion of Text 1, which is the very recommendation Text 2 questions, calling it premature to treat a per-game cap as the best measure. Text 2's author does not need to accept it.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. Text 1 does make this claim, and Text 2 does not dispute it, but Text 2's argument is about whether a per-game cap measures the right thing, not about how easily it can be enforced. The claim is irrelevant to Text 2's reasoning rather than a premise it relies on.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. This is an idea developed in Text 2, which suggests that a weekly total may be more informative. Text 1 recommends only a per-game cap and never mentions combining outings, so the claim cannot be attributed to Text 1.
